body.input: This is VicReq method. So this is co-authored. The first author is a student called Adrien Bard, who is a resident PhD student at FAIR Paris, who is co-advised by me and Jean Ponce, who is a professor at École Normale Superiore, also a research director at INRIA.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So this is a wonderful program in France where PhD students can basically do their PhD in industry. And that's kind of what's happening here.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And this paper is a follow-up on this Barlow-Twin paper by my former postdoc, Stephane Denis, with Li Jing and Eurij Bontar and a bunch of other people from FAIR.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And one of the main criticisms from reviewers is that VicReq is not different enough from Barlow-Twin. But my impression is that Barlow-Twin is with a few bugs fixed essentially. And in the end, this is what people will use.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Right. So...

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But I'm used to stuff that I submit being rejected for a while.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So it might be rejected and actually exceptionally well cited because people use it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Well, it's already cited like a bunch of times.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So, I mean, the question is then to the deeper question about peer review and conferences. I mean, computer science is a field that's kind of unique that the conference is highly prized. That's one.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And it's interesting because the peer review process there is similar, I suppose, to journals, but it's accelerated significantly. Well, not significantly, but it goes fast.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And it's a nice way to get stuff out quickly, peer reviewed quickly, go to present it quickly to the community. So not quickly, but quicker.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But nevertheless, it has many of the same flaws of peer review because it's a limited number of people look at it as bias and the following.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: If you want to do new ideas, you're going to get pushed back. There's self-interested people that kind of can infer who submitted it and kind of be cranky about it, all that kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah. I mean, there's a lot of social phenomena there. There's one social phenomenon, which is that because the field has been growing exponentially, the vast majority of people in the field are extremely junior.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So as a consequence, and that's just a consequence of the field growing. Right. So as the number of the size of the field kind of starts saturating, you will have less of that problem of reviewers being very inexperienced.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: A consequence of this is that young reviewers, I mean, there's a phenomenon which is that reviewers try to make their life easy.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And to make that life easy when reviewing a paper is very simple. You just have to find a flaw in the paper. Right. So basically they see their task as finding flaws in papers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And most papers have flaws, even the good ones. So it's easy to do that. Your job is easier as a reviewer if you just focus on this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But what's important is, is there a new idea in that paper that is likely to influence? It doesn't matter if the experiments are not that great, if the protocol is so-so, things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: As long as there is a worthy idea in it that will influence the way people think about the problem, even if they make it better, eventually, I think that's really what makes a paper useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so this combination of social phenomena creates a disease that has plagued other fields in the past, like speech recognition, where basically people chase numbers on benchmarks.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And it's much easier to get a paper accepted if it brings an incremental improvement on a sort of mainstream, well-accepted method or problem.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And those are, to me, boring papers. I mean, they're not useless, right? Because industry strives on those kind of progress.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But they're not the ones that I'm interested in in terms of new concepts and new ideas. So papers that are really trying to strike new advances generally don't make it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Now, thankfully, we have Archive.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Archive, exactly. And then there's open review type of situations where you – and then, I mean, Twitter is a kind of open review. I'm a huge believer that reviews should be done by thousands of people, not two people.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I agree.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so Archive – like, do you see a future where a lot of really strong papers – it's already the present, but a growing future where it'll just be Archive and you're presenting an ongoing continuous conference called Twitter and slash the Internet.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Slash Archive Sanity – Andre just released a new version – suggests not being so elitist about this particular gating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It's not a question of being elitist or not. It's a question of being basically a recommendation and seal of approvals for people who don't see themselves as having the ability to do so by themselves.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so it saves time. If you rely on other people's opinion and you trust those people or those groups to evaluate a paper for you, that saves you time because you don't have to scrutinize the paper as much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It is brought to your attention. I mean, there's a whole idea of sort of a collective recommender system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So I actually thought about this a lot about 10, 15 years ago because there were discussions at NIPS and we were about to create iClear with Yosha Bengio.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so I wrote a document kind of describing a reviewing system, which basically was you post your paper on some repository, let's say Archive, or now it could be Open Review.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And then you can form a reviewing entity, which is equivalent to a reviewing board of a journal or program committee of a conference.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You have to list the members. And then that group, reviewing entity, can choose to review a particular paper spontaneously or not.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: There is no exclusive relationship anymore between a paper and a venue or reviewing entity. Any reviewing entity can review any paper.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Or may choose not to. And then, you know, give an evaluation. It's not published, not published. It's just an evaluation and a comment, which would be public, signed by the reviewing entity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And if it's signed by a reviewing entity, you know it's one of the members of reviewing entity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So if the reviewing entity is, you know, Lex Friedman's preferred papers, right, you know it's Lex Friedman writing the review.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yes. What, so for me, that's a beautiful system, I think. But what's in addition to that, it feels like there should be a reputation system for the reviewers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: For the reviewing entities, not the reviewers individually.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: The reviewing entities, sure. But even within that, the reviewers too, because there's another thing here. It's not just the reputation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It's an incentive for an individual person to do great. Right now, in the academic setting, the incentive is kind of internal, just wanting to do a good job.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But honestly, that's not a strong enough incentive to do a really good job in reading a paper and finding the beautiful amidst the mistakes and the flaws and all that kind of stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Right. Like if you're the person that first discovered a powerful paper and you get to be proud of that discovery, then that gives a huge incentive to you.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: That's a big part of my proposal, actually, where I describe that as, you know, if your evaluation of papers is predictive of future success, then your reputation should go up as a reviewing entity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So yeah, exactly. I mean, I even had a master's student who was a master's student in library science and computer science actually kind of work out exactly how that should work with formulas and everything.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So in terms of implementation, do you think that's something that's doable?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I mean, I've been sort of talking about this to sort of various people like Andrew McCallum, who started OpenReview.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And the reason why we picked OpenReview for iClear initially, even though it was very early for them, is because my hope was that iClear was eventually going to kind of inaugurate this type of system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So iClear kept the idea of OpenReviews, so where the reviews are published with a paper, which I think is very useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But in many ways, that's kind of reverted to kind of more of a conventional type conferences for everything else.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And I don't run iClear, I'm just the president of the foundation, but people who run it should make decisions about how to run it, and I'm not going to tell them because they are volunteers.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And I'm really thankful that they do that. But I'm saddened by the fact that we're not being innovative enough.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah, me too. I hope that changes.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Because the communication science broadly, but communication, computer science ideas is how you make those ideas have impact, I think.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah, and I think a lot of this is because people have in their mind kind of an objective, which is fairness for authors and the ability to count points basically and give credits accurately.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But that comes at the expense of the progress of science. So to some extent, we're slowing down the progress of science.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And are we actually achieving fairness?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And we're not achieving fairness, you know, we still have biases, you know, we're doing double blind review, but you know, the biases are still there, there are different kinds of biases.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You write that the phenomenon of emergence, collective behavior exhibited by large collection of simple elements, interaction is one of the things that got you into neural nets in the first place.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I love cellular automata. I love simple interacting elements and the things that emerge from them.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Do you think we understand how complex systems can emerge from such simple components that interact simply?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: No, we don't. It's a big mystery. Also, it's a mystery for physicists. It's a mystery for biologists.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You know, how is it that the universe around us seems to be increasing in complexity and not decreasing?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I mean, that is a kind of curious property of physics that despite the second law of thermodynamics, we seem to be, you know, evolution and learning and etc.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Seems to be kind of at least locally to increase complexity, not decrease it. So perhaps the ultimate purpose of the universe is to just get more complex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Have these, I mean, small pockets of beautiful complexity. Does that, do cellular automata, do these kinds of emergence and complex systems give you some intuition or guide your understanding of machine learning systems and neural networks and so on?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Or are these for you right now, disparate concepts?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Well, it got me into it. You know, I discovered the existence of the perceptron when I was a college student.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You know, by reading a book on, it was a debate between Chomsky and Piaget and Seymour Pepper from MIT was kind of singing the praise of the perceptron in that book.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And the first time I heard about the learning machine, right, so I started digging the literature and I found those books,

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: which were basically transcription of, you know, workshops or conferences from the 50s and 60s about self-organizing systems.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So there was a series of conferences on self-organizing systems and these books on this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Some of them are, you can actually get them at the Internet Archive, you know, the digital version.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And there are like fascinating articles in there by, there's a guy whose name has been largely forgotten, Heinz von Förster.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: He's a German physicist who immigrated to the US and worked on self-organizing systems in the 50s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And in the 60s, he created at University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign, he created the biological computer laboratory, BCL, which was all about neural nets.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Unfortunately, that was kind of towards the end of the popularity of neural nets, so that lab never kind of strived very much.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But he wrote a bunch of papers about self-organization and about the mystery of self-organization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: An example he has is you take, imagine you are in space, there's no gravity, you have a big box with magnets in it, okay,

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: you know, kind of rectangular magnets with North Pole on one end, South Pole on the other end.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You shake the box gently and the magnets will kind of stick to themselves and probably form a complex structure, you know, spontaneously.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You know, that could be an example of self-organization.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But you know, you have lots of examples, neural nets are an example of self-organization in many respects.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And it's a bit of a mystery, you know, how, like what is possible with this, you know, pattern formation in physical systems, in chaotic system and things like that, you know, the emergence of life, you know, things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So, you know, how does that happen? So it's a big puzzle for physicists as well.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It feels like understanding this, the mathematics of emergence in some constrained situations might help us create intelligence,

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: like help us add a little spice to the systems because you seem to be able to, in complex systems with emergence, to be able to get a lot from little.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so that seems like a shortcut to get big leaps in performance.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But there's a missing concept that we don't have.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And it's something also I've been fascinated by since my undergrad days.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And it's how you measure complexity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Right. So we don't actually have good ways of measuring or at least we don't have good ways of interpreting the measures that we have at our disposal.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Like how do you measure the complexity of something? Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So there's all those things, you know, like, you know, Kolmogorov, Chaiting, Solomonov, complexity of, you know, the length of the shortest program that would generate a bit string can be thought of as the complexity of that bit string.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I've been fascinated by that concept. The problem with that is that that complexity is defined up to a constant, which can be very large.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: There are similar concepts that are derived from, you know, Bayesian probability theory where, you know, the complexity of something is the negative log of its probability, essentially.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And you have a complete equivalence between the two things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And there you would think, you know, the probability is something that's well defined mathematically, which means complexity is well defined.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But it's not true. You need to have a model of the distribution.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You may need to have a prior if you're doing Bayesian inference and the prior place the same role as the choice of the computer with which you measure Kolmogorov complexity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so every measure of complexity we have has some arbitrariness in it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You know, an additive constant, which can be arbitrarily large.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so, you know, how can we come up with a good theory of how things become more complex if we don't have a good measure of complexity?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Which we need for one way that people study this in the space of biology, the people that study the origin of life or try to recreate life in the laboratory.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And the more interesting one is the alien one is when we go to other planets, how do we recognize this life?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Because, you know, complexity, we associate complexity, maybe some level of mobility with life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You know, we have to be able to like have concrete algorithms for like measuring the level of complexity we see in order to know the difference between life and non-life.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And the problem is that complexity is in the eye of the beholder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So let me give you an example. If I give you an image of the MNIST digits, right, and I flip through MNIST digits,

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: there's obviously some structure to it because local structure, you know, neighboring pixels are correlated across the entire data set.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I imagine that I apply a random permutation to all the pixels, a fixed random permutation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I show you those images. They will look, you know, really disorganized to you, more complex.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: In fact, they're not more complex in absolute terms. They're exactly the same as originally, right?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And if you knew what the permutation was, you know, you could undo the permutation.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Now, imagine I give you special glasses that undo the permutation. Now, all of a sudden, what looked complicated becomes simple.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So if you have two, if you have humans on one end and then another race of aliens that sees the universe with permutation glasses,

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: what we perceive as simple to them is hardly complicated. It's probably heat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah, heat. Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Okay. And what they perceive as simple to us is random fluctuation. It's heat.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah. It's truly in the eye of the beholder. It depends what kind of glasses you're wearing.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Right.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It depends what kind of algorithm you're running in your perception system.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So I don't think we'll have a theory of intelligence, self-organization, evolution, things like this

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: until we have a good handle on a notion of complexity, which we know is in the eye of the beholder.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah, it's sad to think that we might not be able to detect or interact with alien species because we're wearing different glasses.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Because their notion of locality might be different from ours.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: This actually connects with fascinating questions in physics at the moment, like modern physics, quantum physics,

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: like questions about can we recover the information that's lost in a black hole and things like this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And that relies on notions of complexity, which I find is fascinating.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Can you describe your personal quest to build an expressive electronic wind instrument, EWI?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: What is it? What does it take to build it?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Well, I'm a tinkerer. I like building things. I like building things with combinations of electronics and mechanical stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I have a bunch of different hobbies, but probably my first one was little, was building model airplanes and stuff like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And I still do that to some extent. But also electronics. I taught myself electronics before I studied it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And the reason I taught myself electronics is because of music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: My cousin was an aspiring electronic musician and he had an analog synthesizer.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And I was basically modifying it for him and building sequencers and stuff like that for him.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I was in high school when I was doing this.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: How's the interest in progressive rock, like 80s? What's the greatest band of all time, according to Yann LeCun?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: There's too many of them. But it's a combination of

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Mahavishnu Orchestra, Weather Report, yes, Genesis,

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: yes, Genesis, Peter Gabriel, Gentle Giant, things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Great. Okay. So this love of electronics and this love of music combined together.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Right. So I was actually trained to play Baroque and Renaissance music.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And I played in an orchestra when I was in high school and first year of college.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And I played the recorder, crumb horn, a little bit of oboe, things like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So I'm a wind instrument player. But I always wanted to play improvised music, even though I don't know anything about it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And the only way I figured, short of learning to play the saxophone, was to play electronic wind instruments.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So they behave, the fingering is similar to a saxophone, but you have a wide variety of sound because you control the synthesizer with it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So I had a bunch of those going back to the late 80s from either Yamaha or Akai.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: They're both kind of the main manufacturers of those. So they were classically going back several decades.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But I've never been completely satisfied with them because of lack of expressivity.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And those things are somewhat expressive. I mean, they measure the breath pressure, they measure the lip pressure, and you have Baroque's parameters.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You can vary with fingers, but they're not really as expressive as an acoustic instrument.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You hear John Coltrane play two notes and you know it's John Coltrane.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It's got a unique sound, or Miles Davis, right? You can hear it's Miles Davis playing the trumpet because the sound reflects their physiognomy, basically.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: The shape of the vocal tract kind of shapes the sound. So how do you do this with an electronic instrument?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Many years ago, I met a guy called David Wessel. He was a professor at Berklee and created the Center for Music Technology there.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And he was interested in that question. And so I kept kind of thinking about this for many years.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And finally, because of COVID, I was at home. I was in my workshop. My workshop serves also as my Zoom room and home office.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: This is in New Jersey? In New Jersey. And I started really being serious about building my own eWii instrument.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: What else is going on in that New Jersey workshop? Is there some crazy stuff you built or left on the workshop floor, left behind?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: A lot of crazy stuff is electronics built with microcontrollers of various kinds and weird flying contraptions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So you still love flying?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It's a family disease. My dad got me into it when I was a kid. And he was building model airplanes when he was a kid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And he was a mechanical engineer. He taught himself electronics also. So he built his early radio control systems in the late 60s, early 70s.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so that's what got me into, I mean, he got me into kind of engineering and science and technology.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Do you also have an interest in appreciation of flight in other forms like with drones, quadraptors? Or is it model airplane?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Before drones were kind of a consumer product, I built my own with also building a microcontroller with

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: JavaScript and xrmeters for stabilization, writing the firmware for it. And then when it became kind of a standard thing you could buy, it was boring. I stopped doing it. It was not fun anymore.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah, you were doing it before it was cool. What advice would you give to a young person today in high school and college that dreams of doing something big like Yann LeCun?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Let's talk in the space of intelligence, dreams of having a chance to solve some fundamental problem in space of intelligence, both for their career and just in life, being somebody who was a part of creating something special.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So, try to get interested by big questions, things like, you know, what is intelligence? What is the universe made of? What's life all about?

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Even crazy big questions like what's time? Nobody knows what time is.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And then learn basic things like basic methods, either from math, from physics or from engineering. Things that have a long shelf life. Like if you have a choice between like, you know, learning mobile programming on iPhone or quantum mechanics, take quantum mechanics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Because you're going to learn things that you have no idea exist. You may never be a quantum physicist, but you learn about path integrals and path integrals are used everywhere. It's the same formula that you use for, you know, Bayesian integration and stuff like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So the ideas, the little ideas within quantum mechanics, within some of these kind of more solidified fields will have a longer shelf life. They'll somehow use indirectly in your work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Learn classical mechanics like you learn about Lagrangians, for example, which is like a hugely useful concept, you know, for all kinds of different things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Learn statistical physics because all the math that comes out of, you know, for machine learning basically comes out of what's figured out by statistical physicists in the late 19th, early 20th century.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And for some of them, actually more recently, by people like Giorgio Parisi, who just got the Nobel Prize for the replica method, among other things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It's used for a lot of different things. You know, variational inference, that math comes from statistical physics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So a lot of those kind of, you know, basic courses, you know, if you do electrical engineering, you take signal processing, you'll learn about Fourier transforms.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Again, something super useful is at the basis of things like graph neural nets, which is an entirely new sub area of AI machine learning, deep learning, which I think is super promising for all kinds of applications.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Something very promising, if you're more interested in applications, is the applications of AI machine learning and deep learning to science or to science that can help solve big problems in the world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I have colleagues at Meta, at FAIR, who started this project called Open Catalyst.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And it's an open project collaborative. And the idea is to use deep learning to help design new chemical compounds or materials that would facilitate the separation of hydrogen from oxygen.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: If you can efficiently separate oxygen from hydrogen with electricity, you solve climate change.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It's as simple as that, because you cover some random desert with solar panels and you have them work all day, produce hydrogen, and then you ship the hydrogen wherever it's needed.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You don't need anything else. You know, you have controllable power that can be transported anywhere.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So if we have a large scale, efficient energy storage technology like producing hydrogen, we solve climate change.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Here's another way to solve climate change, is figuring out how to make fusion work.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Now, the problem with fusion is that you make a super hot plasma and the plasma is unstable and you can't control it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Maybe with deep learning, you can find controllers that will stabilize plasma and make practical fusion reactors.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I mean, that's very speculative, but it's worth trying because the payoff is huge.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: There's a group at Google working on this led by John Platt.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So control, convert as many problems in science and physics, biology and chemistry into a learnable problem and see if a machine can learn it.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Right. I mean, there's properties of complex materials that we don't understand from first principle, for example.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So if we could design new materials, we could make more efficient batteries.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: We could make maybe faster electronics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: There's a lot of things we can imagine doing or lighter materials for cars or airplanes and things like that, maybe better fuel cells.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I mean, there's all kinds of stuff we can imagine.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: If we had good fuel cells, hydrogen fuel cells, we could use them to power airplanes and transportation wouldn't be or cars.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: We wouldn't have a emission problem, CO2 emission problems for air transportation anymore.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So there's a lot of those things I think where AI can be used.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And this is not even talking about all the sort of medicine, biology and everything like that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Right. You know, like protein folding, you know, figuring out like how can you design your proteins that it sticks to another protein at a particular site because that's how you design drugs in the end.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So, you know, deep learning would be useful.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: All of this. And those are kind of, you know, would be sort of enormous progress if we could use it for that.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Here's an example. If you take this is like from recent material physics, you take a monoatomic layer of graphene.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So it's just carbon on an hexagonal mesh and you make this single single atom thick.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: You put another one on top, you twist them by some magic number of degrees, three degrees or something.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: It becomes superconductor. Nobody has any idea why.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: I want to know how that was discovered. But that's the kind of thing that machine learning can actually discover these things.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Maybe not. But there is a hint perhaps that with machine learning, we would train a system to basically be a phenomenological model of some complex emergent phenomenon, which, you know, superconductivity is one of those.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Where, you know, think this collective phenomenon is too difficult to describe from first principles with the current, you know, the usual sort of reductionist type method.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: But we could have deep learning systems that predict the properties of a system from a description of it after being trained with sufficiently many samples.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: This guy Pascal Fouad at EPFL, he has a startup company that where he basically trained a convolutional net essentially to predict the aerodynamic properties of solids.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And you can generate as much data as you want by just running computational free dynamics.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: So you give like a wing airfoil or something shape of some kind and you run computational free dynamics, you get as a result the drag and lift and all that stuff.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And you can generate lots of data, train a neural net to make those predictions.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And now what you have is a differentiable model of, let's say, drag and lift as a function of the shape of that solid.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And so you can do backgrid and descent, you can optimize the shape so you get the properties you want.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yeah, that's incredible. That's incredible.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: And on top of all that, probably you should read a little bit of literature and a little bit of history for inspiration and for wisdom.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Because after all, all of these technologies will have to work in the human world.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

body.input: Yes. And the human world is complicated.

metadata.title: Podcast: Yann LeCun: Dark Matter of Intelligence and Self-Supervised Learning | Lex Fridman Podcast #258

metadata.title: Podcast: Rick Doblin: Psychedelics | Lex Fridman Podcast #202
